claim: The actin cortex plays a pivotal role in cell division, in generating and maintaining cell polarity and in motility.
source: The actin cortex plays a pivotal role in cell division, in generating and maintaining cell polarity and in motility.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of the actin cortex in cellular processes.

claim: The mechanisms responsible for regulating cortical dynamics in vivo and inducing symmetry breaking are still unclear.
source: Despite extensive research, the mechanisms responsible for regulating cortical dynamics in vivo and inducing symmetry breaking are still unclear.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: A reconstituted system can self-organize into dynamic actin cortices at the inner interface of water-in-oil emulsions.
source: Here we introduce a reconstituted system that self-organizes into dynamic actin cortices at the inner interface of water-in-oil emulsions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental observations.

claim: The artificial system undergoes spontaneous symmetry breaking, driven by myosin-induced cortical actin flows.
source: This artificial system undergoes spontaneous symmetry breaking, driven by myosin-induced cortical actin flows, which appears remarkably similar to the initial polarization of the embryo in many species.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing myosin-dependent symmetry breaking.

claim: The symmetry breaking in the artificial system appears remarkably similar to the initial polarization of the embryo in many species.
source: This artificial system undergoes spontaneous symmetry breaking, driven by myosin-induced cortical actin flows, which appears remarkably similar to the initial polarization of the embryo in many species.
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on the authors' interpretation of their data in relation to known biological phenomena.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton plays a central role in many cellular processes including polarization, cell shape determination, intracellular transport, cell division and movement.
source: The actin cytoskeleton plays a central role in many cellular processes including polarization, cell shape determination, intracellular transport, cell division and movement (Pollard and Cooper, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The structure and function of the cytoskeleton arise from the self-organized dynamics of numerous molecular building blocks.
source: The structure and function of the cytoskeleton arise from the self-organized dynamics of numerous molecular building blocks.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about cytoskeletal organization.

claim: Arp2/3 nucleates branched networks and localizes to cortical actin networks.
source: Among the nucleation-promoting factors, Arp2/3 which nucleates branched networks localizes to cortical actin networks (Machesky et al., 1994) and is essential for cortex formation (Bovellan, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Arp2/3 is essential for cortex formation.
source: Among the nucleation-promoting factors, Arp2/3 which nucleates branched networks localizes to cortical actin networks (Machesky et al., 1994) and is essential for cortex formation (Bovellan, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Amphiphilic ActA spontaneously localized to the water-oil interface following droplet formation.
source: The amphiphilic ActA spontaneously localized to the water–oil interface following droplet formation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation reported in the study.

claim: ActA induced the assembly of a cortical actin network at the inner surface of the aqueous droplets.
source: Upon localization, ActA induced the assembly of a cortical actin network at the inner surface of the aqueous droplets (Figure 1A,D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by microscopy images.

claim: Cortex assembly initiated in patches scattered throughout the interface.
source: Cortex assembly initiated in patches scattered throughout the interface, consistent with the autocatalytic nature of Arp2/3 mediated actin filament nucleation (Mullins and Hansen, 2013; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by microscopy images and consistent with known mechanisms.

claim: The system reached a steady state after approximately 10 minutes, with the formation of thin (approximately 1.5 µm) homogenous actin cortices.
source: The system reached a steady state after ∼10 min, with the formation of thin (∼1.5 µm; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), homogenous actin cortices.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation supported by microscopy data.

claim: The assembled cortices are dynamic, as illustrated by rapid cortical recovery following photobleaching.
source: The assembled cortices are dynamic, as illustrated by the rapid cortical recovery following photobleaching (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by FRAP experiments.

claim: The cortical steady state reflects a balance between actin assembly and disassembly at the interface, as in cells.
source: Thus, the cortical steady state reflects a balance between actin assembly and disassembly at the interface, as in cells (Fritzsche et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, supported by comparison to cellular behavior cited in the literature.

claim: Control experiments with soluble ActA, or in the absence of ActA, resulted in an essentially uniform actin distribution throughout the emulsion droplets, with no apparent cortical localization.
source: Control experiments with soluble ActA, or in the absence of ActA, resulted in an essentially uniform actin distribution throughout the emulsion droplets, with no apparent cortical localization (Figure 1B,C), indicating that cortex formation depends on the localization of a nucleation-promoting factor at the interface.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from control experiments.

claim: Cortex formation depends on the localization of a nucleation-promoting factor at the interface.
source: Control experiments with soluble ActA, or in the absence of ActA, resulted in an essentially uniform actin distribution throughout the emulsion droplets, with no apparent cortical localization (Figure 1B,C), indicating that cortex formation depends on the localization of a nucleation-promoting factor at the interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiments.

claim: The actin network assembled within emulsion droplets incubated at 20°C broke symmetry and formed polar actin caps.
source: The actin network assembled within emulsion droplets incubated at 20°C broke symmetry and formed polar actin caps (Figure 2A), in contrast to the homogenous spherical cortices formed at higher temperature (30°C; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation showing temperature-dependent behavior.

claim: Homogenous spherical cortices formed at 30°C.
source: The actin network assembled within emulsion droplets incubated at 20°C broke symmetry and formed polar actin caps (Figure 2A), in contrast to the homogenous spherical cortices formed at higher temperature (30°C; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation showing temperature-dependent behavior.

claim: The cap formation process developed over approximately 10-20 minutes.
source: The cap formation process developed over ∼10–20 min, with cortical flows initiating at ∼1–4 µm/min (Figure 2E), and slowing down over time, as the cap contracted (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from time-lapse microscopy.

claim: Cortical flows initiated at approximately 1-4 µm/min.
source: The cap formation process developed over ∼10–20 min, with cortical flows initiating at ∼1–4 µm/min (Figure 2E), and slowing down over time, as the cap contracted (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: The position of the actin caps remained stable over much longer time scales, typically exhibiting persistent polarization for hours.
source: Despite this rapid turnover at the molecular level, the position of the actin caps remained stable over much longer time scales, typically exhibiting persistent polarization for hours (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from long-term time-lapse microscopy.

claim: The magnitude of the cortical actin flows and the characteristic length and time scales for polarization observed in the artificial cortices are similar to those seen in developing embryos.
source: Notably, the magnitude of the cortical actin flows and the characteristic length and time scales for polarization observed in our artificial cortices are similar to those seen in developing embryos (Munro et al., 2004; Cowan and Hyman, 2007; Munro and Bowerman, 2009; Mayer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations to literature on embryonic development.

claim: At high temperatures, the fixed bacteria remained distributed throughout the sample, exhibiting comet tail motility, and no overall contraction was observed.
source: At high temperatures, the fixed bacteria remained distributed throughout the sample, exhibiting comet tail motility, and no overall contraction was observed (Figure 2F, right).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the bulk contractility assay.

claim: At lower temperatures, rapid contraction of the entire sample was observed, which concentrated actin filaments in the extract and bacterial comet tails into a narrow strip of actin gel.
source: At lower temperatures, we observed rapid contraction of the entire sample, which concentrated actin filaments in the extract and bacterial comet tails into a narrow strip of actin gel (Figure 2F, left).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the bulk contractility assay.

claim: The transition between non-contractile and contractile behavior occurred abruptly at approximately 25°C.
source: The transition between non-contractile and contractile behavior occurred abruptly at ∼25°C.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the bulk contractility assay.

claim: Cortical polarity developed as a function of time following the temperature shift from 30°C to 20°C.
source: Cortical polarity developed as a function of time following the temperature shift (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from temperature shift experiments.

claim: Within minutes after temperature shift, the homogenous cortical network began to rupture, often in more than one place.
source: Within minutes, the homogenous cortical network began to rupture, often in more than one place (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A; 22′), leading to the formation of gaps in the actin cortex.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from time-lapse microscopy following temperature shift.

claim: After approximately 30 minutes following temperature shift, a polar distribution of actin was observed in all emulsions.
source: After ∼30 min, a polar distribution of actin was observed in all emulsions, characterized in most cases by a single polar cap, similar to the distributions measured in emulsions prepared at 20°C (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from temperature shift experiments.

claim: The ActA density at the water-oil interface increased as a function of the initial bulk ActA concentration used.
source: As expected, the ActA density at the water–oil interface increased as a function of the initial bulk ActA concentration used (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from varying ActA concentrations.

claim: The ActA densities at the interface were higher at 20°C.
source: The ActA densities at the interface were also higher at 20°C, which can be understood from simple thermodynamic considerations; the dynamic localization of ActA at the interface (Figure 2—figure supplement 6) depends on the interplay between enthalpy and entropy which favors localization at lower temperatures.
evidence: This is an experimental observation explained by thermodynamic principles.

claim: Within the range of ActA concentrations examined, the intensity of the actin cortices and their symmetry breaking properties were essentially unaffected by the ActA concentration.
source: However, within the range of ActA concentrations examined, the intensity of the actin cortices and their symmetry breaking properties were essentially unaffected by the ActA concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B,C), suggesting that ActA is in excess.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from varying ActA concentrations.

claim: ActA is in excess in the system.
source: However, within the range of ActA concentrations examined, the intensity of the actin cortices and their symmetry breaking properties were essentially unaffected by the ActA concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B,C), suggesting that ActA is in excess.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The temperature-dependent symmetry breaking observed reflects the changing properties of the cortical actin networks, rather than differences in ActA localization.
source: These results suggest that the temperature-dependent symmetry breaking observed reflects the changing properties of the cortical actin networks, rather than differences in ActA localization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ActA concentration experiments.

claim: Emulsions made from myosin-depleted extracts did not exhibit cortical actin flows and maintained a symmetric actin shell when incubated at 20°C.
source: Emulsions made from myosin-depleted extracts did not exhibit cortical actin flows and maintained a symmetric actin shell when incubated at 20°C (Figure 3A,C), in contrast to the behavior observed at the same temperature in the presence of myosin.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from myosin depletion experiments.

claim: Symmetry breaking was not affected in control experiments with mock immunodepletion.
source: Symmetry breaking was not affected in control experiments with mock immunodepletion (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from control experiments.

claim: Adding purified myosin to myosin-depleted extracts restored symmetry breaking.
source: To further establish the essential role of myosin in the symmetry breaking process, we added different amounts of purified myosin to myosin–depleted extracts and showed that the symmetry breaking is restored (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from myosin add-back experiments.

claim: The cap morphology was dependent on the amount of added myosin.
source: The cap morphology was dependent on the amount of added myosin; as the concentration of myosin increased, we observed more cortices with multiple caps, rather than a single cap (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from varying myosin concentrations.

claim: At higher myosin concentrations (0.66 µM) most of the cortices appear fractured in many places with multiple small interconnected cortical patches which exhibited jittery motion.
source: Moreover, at even higher myosin concentrations (0.66 µM) most of the cortices appear fractured in many places with multiple small interconnected cortical patches which exhibited jittery motion.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from high myosin concentration experiments.

claim: The decrease in the typical size of cortical patches with increasing amounts of myosin is probably due to the decrease in the contractile unit size as a function of myosin concentration.
source: The decrease in the typical size of cortical patches with increasing amounts of myosin is probably due to the decrease in the contractile unit size as a function of myosin concentration (Thoresen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data supported by a citation.

claim: The symmetry breaking observed in the artificial cortices is driven by the same myosin-induced mechanism found in cells.
source: Overall our results suggest that the symmetry breaking observed in our artificial cortices is driven by the same myosin-induced mechanism found in cells (Munro et al., 2004; Mayer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the myosin experiments, supported by citations to cellular studies.

claim: Symmetry breaking can be induced at 30°C by adding crosslinkers.
source: We showed that symmetry breaking can be induced at 30°C by adding crosslinkers (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from crosslinker addition experiments.

claim: Increasing α-actinin concentration led to the formation of polar cortices in a concentration dependent manner.
source: Increasing α-actinin concentration led to the formation of polar cortices in a concentration dependent manner.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from varying α-actinin concentrations.

claim: At low α-actinin concentrations (<4 µM) the cortices remained largely symmetric.
source: At low concentrations (<4 µM) the cortices remained largely symmetric, at intermediate concentrations (4–6 µM) we mostly observed the formation of a single actin cap, while at higher concentrations (8 µM) we often observed multiple actin domains.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from varying α-actinin concentrations.

claim: At intermediate α-actinin concentrations (4-6 µM) mostly the formation of a single actin cap was observed.
source: At low concentrations (<4 µM) the cortices remained largely symmetric, at intermediate concentrations (4–6 µM) we mostly observed the formation of a single actin cap, while at higher concentrations (8 µM) we often observed multiple actin domains.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from varying α-actinin concentrations.

claim: At higher α-actinin concentrations (8 µM) multiple actin domains were often observed.
source: At low concentrations (<4 µM) the cortices remained largely symmetric, at intermediate concentrations (4–6 µM) we mostly observed the formation of a single actin cap, while at higher concentrations (8 µM) we often observed multiple actin domains.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from varying α-actinin concentrations.

claim: Addition of filamin (4 µM) led to the formation of a polar actin cap.
source: Addition of filamin (4 µM) also led to the formation of a polar actin cap.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from filamin addition experiments.

claim: Both α-actinin and filamin were successful at inducing symmetry breaking, highlighting the importance of the overall connectivity of the network rather than the detailed characteristics of individual crosslinkers.
source: Despite the different properties of these crosslinkers, they were both successful at inducing symmetry breaking, highlighting the importance of the overall connectivity of the network rather than the detailed characteristics of individual crosslinkers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the crosslinker experiments.

claim: The cortex, which is under contractile stress, could spontaneously detach from the interface locally.
source: The cortex, which is under contractile stress, could spontaneously detach from the interface locally (Figure 4A; Video 4), as observed in vivo during cellular blebbing (Charras et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an experimental observation showing cell-like behavior.

claim: Detachment of the cortex did not lead to outward bulging of the interface due to the high surface tension of the water-oil interface.
source: Detachment of the cortex did not lead to outward bulging of the interface due to the high surface tension of the water–oil interface in our system (∼700 pN/µm, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is an experimental observation explained by the measured surface tension.

claim: The actin cortex healed over time and a new cortex assembled at the interface within minutes.
source: As in cells (Charras et al., 2006), the actin cortex healed over time and a new cortex assembled at the interface within minutes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation showing recovery after detachment.

claim: The asymmetric actin cortices generated polar forces which could induce reorganization in the interior of the droplet and global deformation of the droplet's shape.
source: In addition, the asymmetric actin cortices generated polar forces which could induce reorganization in the interior of the droplet and global deformation of the droplet's shape (Figure 4B,C; Video 4).
evidence: This is an experimental observation showing force generation.

claim: Shape deformations were observed in approximately 10% of the emulsions.
source: Such deformations were observed in ∼10% of the emulsions, and their incidence increased after longer incubation times compared to the initial polarization event.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: The cytoskeleton exerts a net protrusive force of approximately 20 pN/µm² at the tip of the actin cap.
source: The high curvature at the tip of the actin cap indicates that the cytoskeleton exerts a net protrusive force there, which we estimate to be ∼20 pN/µm2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on curvature measurements.

claim: Away from the tip, on the sides of the actin cap, the local curvature is lower implying that the cytoskeleton is exerting pulling forces on the interface.
source: Away from the tip, on the sides of the actin cap, the local curvature is lower implying that the cytoskeleton is exerting pulling forces on the interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on curvature measurements.

claim: The pulling forces are likely responsible for the accumulation of actin and ActA near the cap.
source: These pulling forces are likely responsible for the accumulation of actin and ActA near the cap (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed accumulation and force measurements.

claim: The average half time for cortical recovery at 30°C was 81 ± 18 seconds.
source: The average half time at 30°C was τ½ = 81 ± 18 s (mean ± STD; N = 18).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FRAP experiments.

claim: The average half time for cortical recovery at 20°C was 73 ± 24 seconds.
source: The average half time at 20°C was τ½ = 73 ± 24 s (mean ± STD; N = 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FRAP experiments.

claim: The average half times at 30°C and at 20°C were not significantly different.
source: The average half times at 30°C and at 20°C were not significantly different (p>0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of FRAP data.

claim: The cortices typically exhibited only partial recovery after bleaching, usually returning to approximately 50% of their initial intensity.
source: The cortices typically exhibited only partial recovery after bleaching, usually returning to ∼50% of their initial intensity.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from FRAP experiments.

claim: The partial recovery appeared to be a result of photodamage during the bleaching step.
source: This partial recovery appeared to be a result of photodamage during the bleaching step.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRAP results.

claim: The surface tension of the water-oil interface is approximately 700 pN/µm.
source: Detachment of the cortex did not lead to outward bulging of the interface due to the high surface tension of the water–oil interface in our system (∼700 pN/µm, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a measured value from pendant-drop assay.

claim: The transition to contractile behavior at lower temperature is primarily due to an increase in the intrinsic crosslinking activity in the system.
source: We hypothesize that the transition to contractile behavior at lower temperature is primarily due to an increase in the intrinsic crosslinking activity in the system.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain their observations.

claim: The increase in crosslinking could emerge from longer dwell times of individual myosin motor heads at low temperature, which would turn the multi-motor myosin filaments into more effective crosslinkers.
source: This increase could emerge from longer dwell times of individual myosin motor heads at low temperature, which would turn the multi-motor myosin filaments into more effective crosslinkers.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the temperature-dependent behavior.

claim: Decreasing temperature could increase the affinity of endogenous actin crosslinkers.
source: Alternatively, decreasing temperature could increase the affinity of endogenous actin crosslinkers.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative mechanism proposed to explain the temperature-dependent behavior.

claim: Actin cortices are close to an instability threshold; small changes in the composition of the system, or in the activity of its components, can lead to dramatic changes in the global characteristics of the system.
source: Overall these findings indicate that actin cortices are close to an instability threshold; small changes in the composition of the system, or in the activity of its components, can lead to dramatic changes in the global characteristics of the system.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Cells are often posed near an instability threshold to enable rapid responses to changing conditions.
source: We believe that this reflects a general organizational principle in cellular systems, whereby cells are often posed near an instability threshold to enable rapid responses to changing conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about cellular organization principles.

claim: The reconstituted system provides novel insights into the complex behavior of the actin cortex in living cells.
source: Our reconstituted system provides novel insights into the complex behavior of the actin cortex in living cells, presenting new opportunities for investigating cortical dynamics, both experimentally and theoretically (Joanny et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the work.

claim: The assembly of dynamic actin cortices requires localization of nucleation factors at the interface.
source: Using this novel reconstituted system we show that the assembly of dynamic actin cortices requires localization of nucleation factors at the interface, and identify the conditions for cortical symmetry breaking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiments.

claim: Symmetry breaking requires myosin motors and sufficient network connectivity.
source: Specifically, we show that symmetry breaking requires myosin motors and sufficient network connectivity, but does not depend upon pre-patterned localization of actin nucleators, the involvement of microtubules (Munro et al., 2004), or any local changes in the properties of the interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the myosin depletion and crosslinker experiments.

claim: Symmetry breaking does not depend upon pre-patterned localization of actin nucleators.
source: Specifically, we show that symmetry breaking requires myosin motors and sufficient network connectivity, but does not depend upon pre-patterned localization of actin nucleators, the involvement of microtubules (Munro et al., 2004), or any local changes in the properties of the interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations showing uniform ActA distribution.

claim: Symmetry breaking does not depend on the involvement of microtubules.
source: Specifically, we show that symmetry breaking requires myosin motors and sufficient network connectivity, but does not depend upon pre-patterned localization of actin nucleators, the involvement of microtubules (Munro et al., 2004), or any local changes in the properties of the interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental system which lacks microtubules.

claim: Symmetry breaking does not depend on any local changes in the properties of the interface.
source: Specifically, we show that symmetry breaking requires myosin motors and sufficient network connectivity, but does not depend upon pre-patterned localization of actin nucleators, the involvement of microtubules (Munro et al., 2004), or any local changes in the properties of the interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental system with a uniform interface.

claim: At 30°C the cortical network appears weakly crosslinked, and hence unable to transmit the contractile stresses generated by myosin motor activity.
source: At 30°C the cortical network appears weakly crosslinked, and hence unable to transmit the contractile stresses generated by myosin motor activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations at different temperatures.

claim: Myosin motors are involved in contractile behavior and symmetry breaking in the cortex of cells.
source: Myosin motors are involved in contractile behavior and symmetry breaking in the cortex of cells (Munro et al., 2004; Cowan and Hyman, 2007; Munro and Bowerman, 2009; Van Der Gucht and Sykes, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Formins nucleate linear filaments and were found to localize to cortical actin networks.
source: Formins, which nucleate linear filaments, were also found to localize to cortical actin networks, yet their role is still not entirely clear (Bovellan, 2012; Fritzsche et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The role of formins in cortical actin networks is still not entirely clear.
source: Formins, which nucleate linear filaments, were also found to localize to cortical actin networks, yet their role is still not entirely clear (Bovellan, 2012; Fritzsche et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement acknowledges uncertainty in current understanding, supported by citations.

claim: Myosin contraction which generates cortical actin flows has been shown to be essential for inducing polarization and defining the anterior-posterior axis during the early stages of embryogenesis in Caenorhabditis elegans and in other species.
source: Comet tail formation is a myosin–independent process driven by actin polymerization (Loisel et al., 1999), whereas cortical symmetry breaking appears to rely on myosin as the main force generating element; myosin contraction which generates cortical actin flows has been shown to be essential for inducing polarization and defining the anterior–posterior axis during the early stages of embryogenesis in Caenorhabditis elegans and in other species (Munro et al., 2004; Mullins, 2010; Munro and Bowerman, 2009; Mayer et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Comet tail formation is a myosin-independent process driven by actin polymerization.
source: Comet tail formation is a myosin–independent process driven by actin polymerization (Loisel et al., 1999), whereas cortical symmetry breaking appears to rely on myosin as the main force generating element
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cortical symmetry breaking appears to rely on myosin as the main force generating element.
source: Comet tail formation is a myosin–independent process driven by actin polymerization (Loisel et al., 1999), whereas cortical symmetry breaking appears to rely on myosin as the main force generating element
evidence: This is a statement of current understanding in the field.

claim: Small changes in the relative amounts of myosin and crosslinkers, or in their activity, can lead to a sharp transition in the overall contractile behavior of reconstituted actin networks.
source: Recent in vitro experiments revealed that small changes in the relative amounts of myosin and crosslinkers, or in their activity, can lead to a sharp transition in the overall contractile behavior of reconstituted actin networks (Bendix et al., 2008; Kohler et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: To emulate cortical dynamics it is essential to incorporate actin turnover dynamics, couple the actin network to a soft interface, and reproduce a cell-like geometry.
source: However, to emulate cortical dynamics it is essential to incorporate actin turnover dynamics, couple the actin network to a soft interface (Murrell and Gardel, 2012), and reproduce a cell-like geometry (Pontani et al., 2009; Pinot et al., 2012; Carvalho et al., 2013b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Myosin is responsible for building tension in actin networks tethered to soft interfaces, and can induce cortical rupture and generate asymmetry.
source: Recent reports (Carvalho et al., 2013a, 2013b) suggest that myosin is responsible for building tension in actin networks tethered to soft interfaces, and can induce cortical rupture and generate asymmetry.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: α-actinin preferentially generates anti-parallel actin bundles.
source: We used two different kinds of actin crosslinkers which are known to localize to cortical actin networks in vivo (Charras et al., 2006), α-actinin which preferentially generates anti-parallel actin bundles and filamin which is a more flexible crosslinker that can bind to disordered actin networks.
evidence: This is a statement of known protein properties.

claim: Filamin is a more flexible crosslinker that can bind to disordered actin networks.
source: We used two different kinds of actin crosslinkers which are known to localize to cortical actin networks in vivo (Charras et al., 2006), α-actinin which preferentially generates anti-parallel actin bundles and filamin which is a more flexible crosslinker that can bind to disordered actin networks.
evidence: This is a statement of known protein properties.

claim: α-actinin and filamin are known to localize to cortical actin networks in vivo.
source: We used two different kinds of actin crosslinkers which are known to localize to cortical actin networks in vivo (Charras et al., 2006), α-actinin which preferentially generates anti-parallel actin bundles and filamin which is a more flexible crosslinker that can bind to disordered actin networks.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Similar behavior was observed with different types of labeled actin.
source: Similar behavior was observed in all cases.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from testing different actin labels.

claim: The total actin concentration in the motility mix is estimated to be approximately 25 µM.
source: We estimate the total actin concentration in the motility mix to be ∼25 µM.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the preparation protocol.
